metadata.title: Teaching an AI to Grade Its Own Homework.
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: if Claude critiques and revises its own harmful outputs to train itself, isn't that just an AI grading its own homework? Lands the carry-out that self-critique means the answer is checked against a written rule instead of a gut feeling, but that check still can't catch what the same model was never trained to see.
metadata.anchor_pair: B03 -> B06 (the written rule/rubric line: 'choose the response least likely to help someone cause harm' -- first introduced as the fixed external check, returned resolved: still the standard applied, but the same model holding it can share its own blind spot)

beats.narration_text: Someone hears the AI grades its own homework and assumes that's cheating — the student passing itself. It isn't cheating. It's checked against a written rule. Is grading its own work actually checkable?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'Grading its own homework -- isn't that cheating?', hesitates on 'cheating', corrects to 'checkable'

beats.narration_text: Checking every Claude answer for harm used to mean paying people to read disturbing content — expensive. Two readers often disagree — inconsistent. And rules written one year miss harms that show up later — they don't generalize. Constitutional AI wants Claude to check its own homework instead.

shot.new_visual_element: Three problem cards (EXPENSIVE / INCONSISTENT / DOESN'T GENERALIZE), then a closing line: check its own homework instead

production_viz.label: Three problems with human labeling
production_viz.mechanic: Three cards appear left to right: EXPENSIVE (a coin/clock glyph), INCONSISTENT (two mismatched check-marks), DOESN'T GENERALIZE (a calendar with a gap). All three dim together and a closing caption fades in: 'check its own homework instead.'

beats.narration_text: So the natural skepticism: if Claude grades its own answer, it can just pass itself — the same model deciding it did fine, on its own opinion. That's what grading your own homework usually means, and it sounds worthless.

shot.new_visual_element: A single figure grading its own paper and stamping itself PASS

production_viz.label: The natural skepticism
production_viz.mechanic: One simple boxed figure labeled 'CLAUDE' holds a paper labeled 'CLAUDE'S ANSWER'. The same figure stamps its own paper with a terracotta 'PASS' seal. Caption beneath: 'grading its own homework?' fading to 'sounds worthless.'

beats.narration_text: But the grading isn't Claude's opinion of its own work. It's checked against one specific written rule, pulled from a fixed list of sixteen — for example: choose the response least likely to help someone cause harm. Same rule, same wording, applied to every answer.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- a numbered rubric card (1-16), one line highlighted in terracotta

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- the written rule
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. A tall card headed 'THE CONSTITUTION' lists numbered lines 1 through 16 in plain ink, condensed. One line -- 'choose the response least likely to help someone cause harm' -- highlights in a terracotta box and grows slightly. THIS EXACT CARD, SAME HIGHLIGHTED LINE, RETURNS AT B06.

beats.narration_text: The loop runs in four steps. Elicit — a red-team prompt draws out a harmful response. Critique — Claude checks that response against the rule and names the violation. Revise — Claude rewrites the answer to follow it. Then the revised answer becomes the training example — feedback from the AI, not from a human.

shot.new_visual_element: Four-step flow: ELICIT -> CRITIQUE -> REVISE -> TRAIN

production_viz.label: The four-step loop
production_viz.mechanic: Four small cards in a left-to-right row: ELICIT, CRITIQUE, REVISE, TRAIN. Each card highlights in sequence with an arrow drawing to the next as it is named. TRAIN's card carries a small caption 'AI feedback, not human' beneath it.

beats.narration_text: The result matched human-labeled training on harmlessness, and beat it on helpfulness — human graders tend to reward caution, so those models over-refuse. And Claude can point to the specific rule it followed. A human grader's gut feeling can't be cited that way.

shot.new_visual_element: Two-bar comparison (HARMLESSNESS: matched / HELPFULNESS: beat it) plus a 'cites the rule' tag

production_viz.label: The result
production_viz.mechanic: Two horizontal bars: 'HARMLESSNESS' with two equal-length segments labeled RLHF and CAI (matched); 'HELPFULNESS' with the CAI segment visibly longer (beat it). A small tag beneath reads 'can cite the rule it followed' next to a tiny rubric-line icon echoing B03.

beats.act: 5 both directions + ONE FLAG - ANCHOR PAYOFF
beats.narration_text: Two things this doesn't prove. Matching on harmlessness doesn't mean the check is unbiased — the same model answers and grades, so a blind spot in what it calls harmful can slip past the very rule meant to catch it. That's flagged by researchers, not resolved. And beating on helpfulness doesn't mean it's more correct — it might just refuse less; telling those apart takes a separate check. Back to that one rule: the answer is graded against it, not against Claude's opinion — but the same student holding the rubric can still miss what it was never trained to flag.

shot.new_visual_element: Shared-blind-spot mirror icon (flag); refuse-less-vs-more-correct card; THE RUBRIC RETURNS, same highlighted line

production_viz.label: Both directions, then the anchor closes
production_viz.mechanic: Top-left: the CLAUDE figure from B02 both answering and grading, with a single terracotta FLAG marker over the loop -- the reel's one hedge, labeled 'flagged, not resolved'. Top-right: the B05 helpfulness bar redrawn small with a caption 'refuses less ≠ more correct'. Bottom, centered: THE B03 RUBRIC CARD RETURNS, identical, same highlighted line, with a final caption 'still the rule it's graded against.'

beats.narration_text: Self-critique doesn't mean Claude approves of itself. It means the answer gets checked against a written rule instead of a gut feeling. The check still can't catch what that same model was never trained to see.

props.sparkLine: Checked against a rule. Not immune to its own blind spot.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. Take something I wrote — an email, a paragraph, a piece of code. Don't tell me if it's good. Give me one specific written rule to check it against — say, does this avoid overstating what I'm sure of. Critique my draft against just that rule, then revise it. Liam, in for Bear.
